Use the large measuring cylinder to pour 100cm of distilled water into the conical flask.

Use the small measuring cylinder to add 6cm of sulfuric acid, 1cm of starch solution and
4cm of aqueous potassium iodide to the flask.
Add 1.0cm of sodium thiosulfate solution from the burette to the mixture in the flask and swirl
to mix.
Several measurements will be taken during this experiment. Once the timer has been started
leave it running until the experiment is complete.
Use the small measuring cylinder to start the reaction by adding 3cm of hydrogen peroxide
solution to the flask. Immediately start your timer and swirl the mixture.
Note the time taken for a blue colour to appear and record the time in the table.
Add a further 0.5cm of sodium thiosulfate solution to the mixture in the conical flask and swirl
until the blue colour disappears.
Note the time when the blue colour reappears and record the time in the table below.
Continue the experiment adding a further 0.5cm of sodium thiosulfate solution at a time until
a total of 4.0cm of sodium thiosulfate solution has been added, noting the times for the blue
colour to appear after each addition and recording the times in the table.

text: You are going to investigate the rate of reaction between hydrogen peroxide and aqueous
potassium iodide. When these chemicals react they form iodine. Sodium thiosulfate solution reacts
with iodine and can be used to show how fast the reaction proceeds.
Read all the instructions carefully before starting the experiment.
Instructions

parts.label: (a)
parts.text:
Use a spatula to place half of solid E into a test-tube.
Add about 10cm of distilled water to the solid and shake the mixture to dissolve.
Divide the solution into three equal portions in three test-tubes and carry out the following
tests.

parts.label: (i)
parts.text:
Add about 1cm of aqueous sodium hydroxide to the first portion of the solution.
Record your observations.

parts.label: (ii)
parts.text:
Add about 1cm of aqueous barium nitrate to the second portion of the solution.
Now add excess dilute nitric acid to the mixture.
Record your observations.

parts.label: (iii)
parts.text:
Pour the third portion of the solution into a boiling tube and add about 1cm of dilute
hydrochloric acid. Warm the mixture gently. Test the gas given off with a piece of filter
paper soaked in aqueous potassium manganate(VII) solution.
Record your observations.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text:
Carry out a flame test on the rest of solid E.
Record your observations.

parts.label: (c)
parts.text:
What conclusions can you draw about solid E?

tests on solid F
Use a spatula to divide solid F into two portions in two test-tubes.

parts.label: (d)
parts.text: Describe the appearance of solid F.

parts.label: (i)
parts.text:
Heat the first portion of solid F, gently then strongly.
Test the gas given off with damp red litmus paper.
Record your observations.

parts.label: (ii)
parts.text:
Let the solid residue cool down for a few minutes. To the residue add a few drops of
copper(II) sulfate solution followed by a few drops of aqueous sodium hydroxide and
shake the mixture.
Record your observations.

parts.label: (f)
parts.text:
Tip the second portion of solid F into a boiling tube.
Add about 3cm of aqueous sodium hydroxide to the boiling tube and heat the mixture gently.
Test the gas given off.
Record your observations.

parts.label: (g)
parts.text: Identify one of the ions in solid F.

text: You are provided with two solids, E and F, which are both water soluble.
Carry out the following tests on the solids, recording all of your observations at each stage.
tests on solid E
Potassium sulfate is the salt made when sulfuric acid is neutralised by potassium hydroxide solution.
The correct amount of potassium hydroxide solution must be added to neutralise all of the sulfuric
acid.
Plan an experiment to obtain pure crystals of potassium sulfate from sulfuric acid and
potassium hydroxide solution.
You are provided with common laboratory apparatus.
